match.reason: The closest bank point, Scarcity, is broader: it covers unlimited wants, the four factors of production and renewable resources, and treats opportunity cost only as one part of that, so it does not teach the focused opportunity-cost point the course needs.

draft.title: Opportunity cost
card: Resources are scarce, so choosing one option means giving up others. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best option given up.
It is only the single next best option, not every option left behind. It is not always money: time, land or effort can be what is given up.
A trade-off is the act of giving up one thing to get another. Weighing the opportunity cost shows what each choice really costs.
In a cost-benefit analysis, a person or government compares the costs and benefits of a choice. A choice is worth making when its benefits outweigh its costs, including the opportunity cost.
draft.remember: Every choice has a cost: the next best option you gave up.

a.q: Ravi has a free Saturday. He could work a shift for $120, go to a football match, or study. He picks the match and would have studied second. What is his opportunity cost?
opts: The study time he gave up
The $120 he would have earned
The study time and the $120 together
The cost of the match ticket
a.why: Opportunity cost is the next best option given up, and for Ravi that is studying. The $120 shift was a third choice, so it is not counted. Adding it would count more than the single next best option.
a.clue: Which option came second in his ranking?

b.q: A council in Ballarat has land for one project. It could build a library, which it ranks first, or a car park, which it ranks second, or a skate park, which it ranks third. What is the opportunity cost of choosing the library?
opts: The car park
The skate park
The car park and the skate park
Nothing, as the library was its first choice
b.why: The opportunity cost is the next best option given up, which is the car park. The skate park is also given up but ranks lower, so it is not counted. Choosing the best option still has an opportunity cost, because something is given up.
b.clue: Only the second-ranked option counts, even when you chose the top one.

a.best: The study time he gave up

problems.detail: The clue ('Only the second-ranked option counts, even when you chose the top one') states the rule and points straight at the car park, so a student can answer without understanding opportunity cost.
